evidence: Cic. Tusc. 5.116: nē strīdōrem quidem serrae, tum cum acuitur
Levi–Bini p. 7, s.v. arrotare: acuere; exacuere
terms.comment: The plain verb, of knives, axes, saws, and tools; on the whetstone is cōte (see “whetstone”). Its participle acūtus is “sharp”. By a figure it sharpens the wits and spurs a person on (see “stimulate”).

terms.gloss: sharpen well, bring to a point
evidence: Verg. G. 1.264: exacuunt aliī vallōs furcāsque bicornīs

phrases.latin: Culter hebes est; cōte eum acuam.
phrases.english: The knife is blunt; I’ll sharpen it on the whetstone.
Don’t touch: I’ve just sharpened the knife.

phrases.latin: Tum etiam per lūcubrātiōnem ferrāmenta acuere et ad ea facere vel facta manūbria aptāre
phrases.english: Then too, working by lamplight, one can sharpen the tools and make handles for them, or fit those already made

phrases.latin: ‘At vōcem citharoedī nōn audiunt.’ Nē strīdōrem quidem serrae, tum cum acuitur
phrases.english: ‘But they cannot hear the singer to the lyre.’ Nor the screech of a saw either, when it is being sharpened

sources: Lewis & Short: acuo · Lewis & Short: exacuo · Lewis & Short: cos
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 7, s.v. arrotare.
